findings.title: Define caller-tuple uniqueness across installation replacement
findings.evidence: The explicit registry restriction permits one enabled installation per issuer/project/subject/client/resource tuple. The verified token contains no installation identity or binding generation; the application constructs those from current registry state. The surrounding requirements for distinct client IDs, immutable bindings and duplicate-match rejection do not explicitly establish whether disabled or retired bindings permanently reserve their tuple.
findings.consequence: An implementation could disable installation A, register B with the same tuple, then map A's still-valid token to B's current generation. Testing stale caller contexts or cursors would not catch this fresh authentication with unchanged token bytes. The design needs an unambiguous temporal interpretation of its same-client isolation guarantee.
findings.required_change: Define the first profile's replacement rule. The smallest repair is to reserve each tuple to one installation identity across its retained history and require a distinct qualified client identity for a replacement installation. Alternatively, specify an independently established credential-generation distinction. Explicitly distinguish re-enabling the same installation from replacing it, and add an unchanged-old-token replacement/restart test.

findings.title: Make restart-time evidence an explicit implementation prerequisite
findings.evidence: The design correctly requires holding on clock rollback or an unavailable trustworthy time bound. Existing mcp-auth uses SystemTime and jsonwebtoken wall-clock timestamps at rust/crates/mcp-auth/src/main.rs:107-114,157-176. Those observations alone do not establish elapsed downtime or trustworthy time after restart.
findings.consequence: A synthetic rollback test or persisted last-observed timestamp could be mistaken for proof that grants cannot be extended across an unobserved restart interval.
findings.recommendation: At the implementation checkpoint, identify the source and owner of the accepted time bound and the restart hold/revalidation behavior. Include a restart after actual expiry with the wall clock restored to a plausible earlier value. Keep synthetic-clock qualification distinct from production clock assurance.

findings.title: Allocate guarded response emission explicitly to A2.1
findings.evidence: The common contract correctly includes response disclosure, but A2.1's summarized acceptance lists read/denial, disable/restart/CAS and profile isolation while A2.2 explicitly names invalidation ordering. Existing AH returns application data before transport emission: rust/crates/work-engine-server/src/main.rs:560-581 and 767-781.
findings.consequence: A builder could underestimate the immediate slice as ingress authorization plus a read adapter, leaving response fencing and its race evidence for the callback slice.
findings.recommendation: Name guarded response emission and both response/invalidation serial orderings in A2.1's acceptance and allocation. Callback ordering remains A2.2 work. This clarifies the already stated invariant rather than requiring a particular locking route.

assessment.ownership: The proposed separation is defensible: mcp-auth owns cryptographic/profile validation; connector-policy owns installation access and grant semantics; existing domain and delivery owners retain their state machines and effect accounting.
assessment.capabilities: The subject accurately distinguishes Boolean legacy authentication, local AH operation HTTP, stdio MCP and fixture-only native delivery from the new capabilities requiring implementation. No existing generic OAuth callback engine or live issuer compatibility is established.
assessment.trust_boundaries: Scope intersection, namespaced caller identity, private authority construction, trusted resource/destination registration, enrichment dependencies, replay ownership and legacy-profile isolation are addressed. Issuer token-class separation and upstream consent revocation are correctly treated as separate, unestablished deployment facts.
assessment.state_and_ordering: CAS revisions are not confused with semantic authority. Lost acknowledgements, historical reads, tombstones and catastrophic control-repository restoration have appropriate distinctions. The collection/disclosure admission invariant is sound, and the design rejects unlocked Boolean permits. The actual effect-owner composition remains proposed work.
assessment.structure_vs_routes: The subject generally separates required outcomes from optional mechanics. Per-installation guards, holding a guard during bounded I/O and the selected persistence adapter are implementation choices; current authorization and ordering at actual effect admission are the structural requirements.
